chapter: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
title: Passing Black motorists refuse to tow; a white farmer does
summary: Black drivers with wood slow past for fear; a white man with a boy tows them to a garage and refuses pay.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When we got passed that little place, I guess it was three or four--you couldn't call it a street, a little section there, with shotguns and rocks. And so there we were, but a lot of time, I mean you talk about the good lord looking out for us, here comes some other negroes by which had a load of wood on them, and they stopped at this station (inaudible), and they stopped and got some gas, so I got out on the side, and flagged them down so they could tow us to this garage that he was talking about and when I got out they just slowed down and changed gear and said, they'll get us if we help you. So there we were.

So I sat back down and in a little while, a white fellow and a little boy about eight or nine years old was going in the other direction from where we were heading and I flagged him. He had a tow chain and everything in his truck and I asked him how far is the next town from here, a garage where I could get work done, I think my water pump was out. He said about ten or twelve miles. I said I would like you to tow the bus there, I'll pay you for your time. He said I'll tow you there but you can't pay me.

He turned right on around, had a chain in there, hooked it on and I rode on along with him, didn't need any explanation or nothing. He knew exactly something had gone on. He just said I wonder when my friends around here will ever wake up.
In Florida, in Lee County. I don't know the name of the town,
lord knows it had some kind of name, but I know it was Lee County.
(Side A of Tape 3 ends at this point. Transcript will continue in accordance with Side B.)
